alternatives.argument: Calegari §4.2 (printed p. 141) works with transversals to the leaves; Meinrenken Definition 2.6(b) and Leiden Definition 2.2 define a transversal as a q-dimensional submanifold transverse to all leaves, the direct-sum formulation used here.

Leiden Definition and Lemma 2.3 constructs the holonomy map along a leaf path exactly by a finite chart chain (with the single-chart case proved first); Calegari §4.2 (printed pp. 141–142) composes the plaque identifications h_i along a chart chain.

Leiden Definition and Lemma 2.3 states that the holonomy map does not depend on the intermediate transversals; Calegari §4.2 refines to smaller neighbourhoods as necessary; Meinrenken Definition 2.6 says the germ is unchanged when the leaf path and transversals are varied sufficiently close.

Calegari §4.2 (printed p. 142) breaks a homotopy into a sequence of homotopies supported in small product charts and concludes that holonomy transport is well defined on relative homotopy classes; Leiden Proposition 2.4(2) states homotopy invariance.
Leiden Proposition 2.4(1) gives hol_{R,T}(βα)=hol_{R,S}(β)∘hol_{S,T}(α); Calegari Theorem 4.4 states that holonomy transport is a homomorphism to the groupoid of germs.

Leiden Definition 2.5 defines the holonomy group as the image of hol_{T,T}:π1(L,x)→Diff_x(T) and proves conjugacy under change of transversal; Calegari §4.2 (printed p. 141) defines the holonomy representation into germs; Meinrenken Definition 2.7(b) states the same.

Leiden §1.3.5/§3.2–3.3 supply the covering-space and groupoid background; Proposition 3.17(4) is the universal-cover analogue for the monodromy groupoid, and the kernel-of-holonomy refinement is assembled on this page from the covering-space action lemma and the holonomy representation (kernels are conjugacy-invariant).
Leiden Definition 3.15(1) and Meinrenken Definition 2.8(a) define the monodromy groupoid by homotopy classes of leaf paths with concatenation.

Leiden Definition 3.15(2) and Meinrenken Definition 2.8(b) define the holonomy groupoid by holonomy classes of leaf paths; Leiden Proposition 3.17(1) gives the natural map from the monodromy groupoid.

Meinrenken's discussion following Definition 2.8 identifies the vertex groups of Hol(F); Leiden Definition 2.5 and Proposition 3.17(3) supply the holonomy-group and discreteness identifications used here.

Leiden §1.3.2 (Definition 1.16 and its proof) proves that a transverse map pulls the foliation back to a foliation and derives codim f*F=codim F and Tf*F=(Tf)^{-1}(TF); the constant-rank kernel description used here is the smooth-distribution form of the same computation.

Leiden §1.3.3 proves the quotient-foliation statement for covering-space actions (Hausdorff quotient, induced atlas, leaves L/G_L, codim and T(π)(TF)); Meinrenken Example 2.3 and Calegari Example 4.7 give the standard instances.

Leiden §1.3.4 (suspension of a diffeomorphism) and §1.3.5 (flat bundle B̃×_{π1(M)}F) give the construction; Meinrenken Example 2.3 states the associated-bundle form with leaves covering the base; Calegari Example 4.2 treats the circle-bundle case.

sources.title: Danny Calegari, Foliations and the Geometry of 3-Manifolds (Oxford Mathematical Monographs; author-hosted PDF)
sources.locator: §4.2, printed pp. 140–143 (PDF pp. 149–152) in full; §4.3, printed pp. 144–147 (PDF pp. 153–156), Examples 4.7–4.10.
sources.reading_verification: Downloaded the complete author-hosted book PDF (371 PDF pages) and extracted it page by page with mutool. Read §4.2 "Foliated bundles and holonomy" end to end on PDF pp. 149–152: Example 4.2 (foliated circle bundles as quotients of Σ̃×S¹ by π1(Σ)), the unique path lifting and completeness discussion, Theorem 4.3 (complete foliated F-bundles up to isomorphism correspond to conjugacy classes of homomorphisms π1(B)→Homeo(F)), the construction of the holonomy representation via the normal disk bundle of a leaf, holonomy transport along a chart chain with its homotopy-invariance argument ('the map h′ ... agrees with h ... holonomy transport is well-defined on relative homotopy classes'), Theorem 4.4 (holonomy transport is a homomorphism to the groupoid of germs of self-homeomorphisms of a transversal), Theorem 4.5 (Reeb stability for spherical leaves in co-oriented foliations), and the Remark and Example 4.6 on closed leaves and harmonic measure. Read §4.3 from PDF p. 153: Example 4.7 (the Reeb component as the quotient of the upper half-space minus the origin by the properly discontinuous dilation p↦2p, with the horizontal foliation descending), Example 4.8 (spiral leaves), Example 4.9 (spinning) and the opening of Example 4.10 (smooth filling) to classify the three-manifold constructions as not consumed here.

contents.name: Example 4.2 (foliated circle bundles: the quotient of Σ̃×S¹ by the diagonal π1(Σ)-action and its transverse foliation)
Unique path lifting and the completeness condition for foliated bundles (leaf projections to the base are coverings)
contents.reason: Completeness is a property of the foliated-bundle holonomy used to classify complete bundles; the suspension of this page is not claimed to be complete, and no DT-29 item uses completeness.

contents.name: Theorem 4.3 (complete foliated F-bundles over B correspond to conjugacy classes of homomorphisms π1(B)→Homeo(F))
contents.reason: The classification needs the compact-open topology on Homeo(F) and a completeness hypothesis; this page builds the smooth suspension for Diff(F)-representations and does not classify complete bundles.

contents.name: The holonomy representation, defined by pulling the foliation back to the normal disk bundle of a leaf
Holonomy transport along a path: chart-chain construction and independence of the chain
Homotopy invariance of holonomy transport (paths homotopic relative endpoints induce the same germ)
Theorem 4.4 (Holonomy transport is a homomorphism to the groupoid of germs of self-homeomorphisms of a transversal)
Theorem 4.5 (Reeb stability: a co-oriented foliation with a spherical leaf is the product foliation of S²×S¹)
contents.reason: The compact-leaf stability theorem and its spherical-leaf specialisation are the subject of the DT-30 pair, which consumes the holonomy constructions of this page as prerequisites.

contents.name: Remark on closed leaves under finite covers and Example 4.6 (harmonic measure preserved on average by holonomy transport)
contents.reason: Invariant transverse measures and their comparison with tautness belong to the Godbillon–Vey/tautness pair; no DT-29 claim uses transverse measures.

contents.name: Example 4.7 (Reeb component as the quotient of the upper half-space minus the origin by the properly discontinuous dilation action; the horizontal foliation descends)
Examples 4.8–4.10 (spiral leaves; spinning; smooth filling of foliated solid tori)
contents.reason: Three-dimensional foliation engineering that builds Reeb components and fills foliated solid tori; the quotient and suspension models of this page close DT-29 without it, and no DT-30/DT-31 design item consumes these constructions.

contents.name: Example 2.2 (mapping torus of a diffeomorphism: the Z-invariant foliation descends; a periodic point gives a circle leaf, an aperiodic point a line leaf)
Example 2.3 (a proper action of a discrete group preserving a foliation: the quotient inherits a foliation)
Example 2.3 continued (the associated bundle B̃×_Λ Q of a π1-action: the diagonal action leaves the vertical foliation invariant and its leaves are coverings of B)
Example 2.4 (linear foliation of the two-torus; rational slope gives a manifold leaf space, irrational slope a pathological one)
Example 2.5 (Reeb foliation of the three-sphere)
contents.reason: The Reeb foliation is the canonical unstable compact-leaf model and belongs to the stability pair; DT-29 records only the holonomy machinery it illustrates.

contents.name: Definition 2.6(a) (foliation path and foliation loop, i.e. a path in a single leaf)
Definition 2.6(b) (a transversal as a q-dimensional submanifold transverse to all leaves)
Definition 2.6 continued (holonomy of a leaf path is the germ φ_γ:N→N′; it is unchanged under homotopies of the path and independent of the transversals)
Definition 2.7 (monodromy group Mon(F,m)=π1(L,m); holonomy group Hol(F,m) as the image in the germs of diffeomorphisms of a local transversal; Hol is the quotient of Mon by loops of trivial holonomy)
Definition 2.8(a) (monodromy groupoid Mon(F): triples (m′,m,[γ]) with [γ] a homotopy class of leaf paths, multiplication by concatenation)
Definition 2.8(b) (holonomy groupoid Hol(F): the same with holonomy classes of leaf paths) and the statement that its vertex groups are the holonomy groups
The isotropy statement Hol(F)(m,m)=image of the holonomy representation (vertex groups of the holonomy groupoid are the holonomy groups)
Proposition 2.9 (Mon(F) and Hol(F) are possibly non-Hausdorff manifolds, with the chart construction) and Remark 2.10 (non-uniqueness of limits; independent Hausdorff behaviour of the two groupoids)
Exercises 2.1–2.4 (fibre foliations of ℝ³∖{0}; Reeb foliation of S³; S³ minus the cores; S²×S¹: the four combinations of Hausdorff and non-Hausdorff groupoids)
contents.reason: These exercises ask for computations of the étale topology of the arrow spaces of Reeb-type foliations; the page records the non-Hausdorffness phenomenon without constructing that topology.

contents.name: §2.4 Appendix: Haefliger's foliation topology and the étale germ groupoid of a foliation
contents.reason: The Haefliger germ groupoid requires the foliation topology and étale-groupoid machinery; the design deliberately keeps this page away from that level of structure.

sources.title: Leiden NCG seminar, Noncommutative Geometry of Foliations (2023 seminar notes, complete 53-page PDF)
sources.locator: §1.3, printed pp. 8–10 (PDF pp. 9–11): product, pullback, quotient, suspensions, flat bundles, Reeb; §2.1, printed pp. 11–14 (PDF pp. 12–15): holonomy; §3.2, printed pp. 20–21 (PDF pp. 21–22): groupoids of foliations. Corroborating exposition derived from the Moerdijk–Mrčun book.
sources.reading_verification: Downloaded the complete 53-page seminar-note PDF and extracted it page by page with mutool. Read §1.3 "Constructions and more examples" on PDF pp. 9–11: 1.3.1 product foliations; 1.3.2 Definition 1.16 (a map transverse to a foliation), the Haefliger-structure proof that the pullback data define a foliation, the surjectivity computation, and the conclusions codim f*F=codim F, Tf*F=(Tf)^{-1}(TF); 1.3.3 quotient foliations of covering-space actions (free properly discontinuous action preserving the foliation, induced atlas, leaves L/G_L, codim and tangent distribution), Example 1.17 (Kronecker foliation as the quotient of the suspension foliation of s(x,y)=x−ϑy by ℤ²) and Example 1.18 (Möbius band foliation); 1.3.4 suspensions of diffeomorphisms; 1.3.5 flat bundles B̃×_{π1(M)}F and the invariance of the submersion foliation; 1.3.6 the beginning of the Reeb construction. contents.name: 1.3.1 Product foliations
contents.support: The product foliation is the trivial-representation case of the suspension construction, which the definition records.

Example 1.18 (the Möbius band foliation, with the middle leaf winding once and every other leaf winding twice)

contents.reason: The transverse/tangent-to-boundary vocabulary and the Reeb component are used by the stability and secondary-class pairs, not by any holonomy claim of DT-29.

contents.name: §2.1.1 Motivation: the Poincaré return map of a periodic orbit of a flow
contents.support: The remark records that the return map is the special periodic-orbit case that motivates, but is not part of, the general germ-valued holonomy.

Definition 2.1 continued (the group structure of the germs of local diffeomorphisms fixing a point)

contents.reason: The contracting-holonomy computation is the instability model used by the Reeb stability and Godbillon–Vey pairs, not by any DT-29 claim.

alternatives.argument: Leiden Example 1.17 constructs the Kronecker foliation as the quotient of the suspension foliation of x−ϑy and Example 2.7 records that simply connected leaves have trivial holonomy; Meinrenken Example 2.4 describes the rational versus irrational leaf structure; Calegari §4.2 gives the dense-line picture.

Leiden Example 1.18 constructs the Möbius foliation and Example 2.8 computes the middle-leaf holonomy group ℤ/2 generated by the reflection and the trivial holonomy of all other leaves; Meinrenken Example 2.2 gives the mapping-torus picture used here.

Meinrenken Example 2.2 identifies leaves of the mapping torus (circle leaf for a periodic point, line leaf otherwise); Calegari §4.2 and Leiden §1.3.4 give the suspension construction and its holonomy transport used to compute the return germ.

Leiden §1.3.5 constructs flat bundles B̃×_{π1(M)}F and identifies horizontal leaves; Meinrenken Example 2.3 gives the associated-bundle form; Calegari Example 4.2 gives the circle-bundle instance used for the linear case.

Leiden §1.3.2 supports the transverse pullback convention and rank identity, not this locally repaired failure witness. For f(t)=(0,t²) into the horizontal foliation, df_t(v)=(0,2tv), so (df_t)^{-1}(TF)={0} for t≠0 and T_0R at 0; the inverse-image rank is nonconstant. This exact arithmetic refutes the inference without transversality.

Leiden Example 2.8 supplies the Möbius holonomy computation (generator ↦ reflection, square ↦ identity) on which the example-independent witness rests; Meinrenken Definition 2.7(b) states that the holonomy group is the quotient of the monodromy group by trivially-holonomic loops.

Example 2.3 (a proper action of a discrete group preserving a foliation: the quotient inherits a foliation)
Example 2.3 continued (the associated bundle B̃×_Λ Q of a π1-action: the diagonal action leaves the vertical foliation invariant and its leaves are coverings of B)
Example 2.4 (linear foliation of the two-torus; rational slope gives a manifold leaf space, irrational slope a pathological one)
Example 2.5 (Reeb foliation of the three-sphere)
contents.reason: The Reeb foliation is the canonical unstable compact-leaf model and belongs to the stability pair; DT-29 records only the holonomy machinery it illustrates.

contents.name: Definition 2.6(a) (foliation path and foliation loop, i.e. a path in a single leaf)
Definition 2.6(b) (a transversal as a q-dimensional submanifold transverse to all leaves)
Definition 2.6 continued (holonomy of a leaf path is the germ φ_γ:N→N′; it is unchanged under homotopies of the path and independent of the transversals)
Definition 2.7 (monodromy group Mon(F,m)=π1(L,m); holonomy group Hol(F,m) as the image in the germs of diffeomorphisms of a local transversal; Hol is the quotient of Mon by loops of trivial holonomy)
Definition 2.8(a) (monodromy groupoid Mon(F): triples (m′,m,[γ]) with [γ] a homotopy class of leaf paths, multiplication by concatenation)
Definition 2.8(b) (holonomy groupoid Hol(F): the same with holonomy classes of leaf paths) and the statement that its vertex groups are the holonomy groups
The isotropy statement Hol(F)(m,m)=image of the holonomy representation (vertex groups of the holonomy groupoid are the holonomy groups)
Proposition 2.9 (Mon(F) and Hol(F) are possibly non-Hausdorff manifolds, with the chart construction) and Remark 2.10 (non-uniqueness of limits; independent Hausdorff behaviour of the two groupoids)
Exercises 2.1–2.4 (fibre foliations of ℝ³∖{0}; Reeb foliation of S³; S³ minus the cores; S²×S¹: the four combinations of Hausdorff and non-Hausdorff groupoids)
contents.reason: These exercises ask for computations of the étale topology of the arrow spaces of Reeb-type foliations; the page records the non-Hausdorffness phenomenon without constructing that topology.

contents.name: §2.4 Appendix: Haefliger's foliation topology and the étale germ groupoid of a foliation
contents.reason: The Haefliger germ groupoid requires the foliation topology and étale-groupoid machinery; the design deliberately keeps this page away from that level of structure.

contents.reason: The contracting-holonomy computation is the instability model used by the Reeb stability and Godbillon–Vey pairs, not by any DT-29 claim.

contents.name: Example 4.2 (foliated circle bundles: the quotient of Σ̃×S¹ by the diagonal π1(Σ)-action and its transverse foliation)
Unique path lifting and the completeness condition for foliated bundles (leaf projections to the base are coverings)
contents.reason: Completeness is a property of the foliated-bundle holonomy used to classify complete bundles; the suspension of this page is not claimed to be complete, and no DT-29 item uses completeness.

contents.name: Theorem 4.3 (complete foliated F-bundles over B correspond to conjugacy classes of homomorphisms π1(B)→Homeo(F))
contents.reason: The classification needs the compact-open topology on Homeo(F) and a completeness hypothesis; this page builds the smooth suspension for Diff(F)-representations and does not classify complete bundles.

contents.name: The holonomy representation, defined by pulling the foliation back to the normal disk bundle of a leaf
Holonomy transport along a path: chart-chain construction and independence of the chain
Homotopy invariance of holonomy transport (paths homotopic relative endpoints induce the same germ)
Theorem 4.4 (Holonomy transport is a homomorphism to the groupoid of germs of self-homeomorphisms of a transversal)
Theorem 4.5 (Reeb stability: a co-oriented foliation with a spherical leaf is the product foliation of S²×S¹)
contents.reason: The compact-leaf stability theorem and its spherical-leaf specialisation are the subject of the DT-30 pair, which consumes the holonomy constructions of this page as prerequisites.

contents.name: Remark on closed leaves under finite covers and Example 4.6 (harmonic measure preserved on average by holonomy transport)
contents.reason: Invariant transverse measures and their comparison with tautness belong to the Godbillon–Vey/tautness pair; no DT-29 claim uses transverse measures.
